articles.title: macOS 26 Tahoe Guide: All the new features in macOS Tahoe, including the latest update
articles.subtitle: Macworld Like its counterparts on the other Apple devices, on September 15, 2025 macOS got a brand new look along with a new name: macOS 26.
articles.author: Macworld
articles.content:
Like its counterparts on the other Apple devices, on September 15, 2025 macOS got a brand new look along with a new name: macOS 26. Because Apple is aligning the names of all the operating systems this year, the new version of macOS is called macOS 26 rather than macOS 16. It also takes the name Tahoe, inspired by the lake, beaches, and the ski resorts of that area of California.

Along with a big redesign, macOS 26 brings new Continuity features to bring your iPad, iPhone, and Mac even closer together, a brand new Phone app, and more. Spotlight also gets its biggest ever update with the ability to action things like sending emails directly from Spotlight.

macOS Tahoe might have launched, but Apple is continuing development with new features being added every couple of months – the latest update being macOS 26.6.2. You can get a first look at the new upcoming features via Apple’s developer and public betas, which are available to download if you join the beta program (we explain how to do so below).

You will find all the things you need to know about macOS Tahoe and all its new features below, including which Macs are compatible with macOS 26 and the new features you can expect, including what’s been added since the September launch, and what’s coming in the next update. Stay tuned to this superguide for everything you need to know about macOS 26 Tahoe.

macOS 26 Tahoe: Summary

The new version of macOS, called macOS 26 Tahoe, was released on September 15 2025.

The lates t version–macOS 26.6.2–arrived on Augut 17, 2026.

macOS 26 Tahoe is still being developed and you can access new features before they are launched via the Developer and Public Betas.

Tahoe runs on Macs released since 2019. macOS 26 Tahoe runs on all M-series Macs, but it runs on a small number of Intel-powered models. Apple has confirmed that macOS Tahoe will be the last macOS version to support Intel-powered Macs; from macOS 27 Intel Macs will not be supported.

With its new Liquid Glass interface, macOS 26 has its biggest design change since 2013.

New features in macOS Tahoe include more options for personalization, improvements to Spotlight and Shortcuts app, and the introduction of a Phone app on the Mac and all the associated features.

What is the latest version of macOS 26 Tahoe?

Latest version of macOS is macOS Tahoe 26.6.2, which arrived on August 17, 2026.

Apple released the first version of macOS 26 Tahoe on September 15, 2025. The release coincided with the iOS 26 update. Since then the following updates to Tahoe have been issued by Apple:

articles.title: Jungle Shot 11 Music Videos in Four Days with Apple Creator Studio
articles.subtitle: Source: Apple. Today, Jungle released their fifth studio album, Sunshine. Alongside the release, Apple published a look at how the band used Apple Creator Studio to film 11 music videos in just four days, an impressive feat no matter the technology used.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Today, Jungle released their fifth studio album, Sunshine. Alongside the release, Apple published a look at how the band used Apple Creator Studio to film 11 music videos in just four days, an impressive feat no matter the technology used.

The band’s toolbox included Logic Pro, Final Cut Pro, and Pixelmator Pro to capture the series of signature one-shot take videos. According to the App Store feature on the band’s process, Logic Pro was where the entire album was produced. The app’s Varispeed feature was also used to shift the tempo of songs while maintaining pitch as they shot the videos.

Final Cut Pro’s Magnetic Mask was used to composite footage quickly. Jungle’s Tom McFarland told Apple:

Final Cut Pro is like a magic sword. There’s one shot for the track ‘Romeo II,’ where the camera accidentally caught some of the lighting rig. With five clicks, the editor was able to paint it out. It just automatically knows.

Pixelmator Pro on the iPad with an Apple Pencil and Mac enabled the band’s team to add artwork and posters to the final product, too.

But of all the quotes from the band, J Lloyd’s comment really struck a chord with me:

We didn’t have to worry about the tech. We could just focus on getting the design right. I could pick up the iPad between takes and keep sketching on Pixelmator Pro, and it all just worked.

I love apps, or I wouldn’t write about them every day, but what I love even more is the creativity they enable. Getting a glimpse of how one of my favorite bands uses some of the same tools I do was a treat.

articles.title: Apple’s China AI strategy now includes training its own custom model, per report
articles.subtitle: china Apple Intelligence Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:

Apple Intelligence

Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.

Reuters reports that three sources described the China-specific model as a departure from Apple’s strategy of relying on third-party models.

Alibaba reportedly supported the model’s training, though neither company commented.

Models including ChatGPT and Claude are unavailable in mainland China, making Apple’s strategy there different from its approach in other major markets for now.

The development follows Alibaba confirming its Apple partnership in February 2025. More recently, China’s internet regulator registered Apple Intelligence for use on iPhones.

Previous reporting said Alibaba’s Qwen model and technology from Baidu would be incorporated into the localized system.

Reuters says it remains unclear how Apple’s new model will work alongside those third-party models. Apple Intelligence is expected to reach China in the coming months following an iOS update, according to the report.

Elsewhere, Apple’s overhauled Siri AI is scheduled to launch publicly with iOS 27 this fall where available.

It will initially support select English variants, while iPhone and iPad availability in the EU is delayed. China’s timeline remains unconfirmed.

articles.title: Toymaker Mattel launches a new game studio with a focus on Roblox and Fortnite that could signal a growing shift in where studios spend money
articles.subtitle: In chasing the money, Mattel Game Studios doesn't seem particularly interested in Steam or consoles.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
10 billion hours in Roblox Toy company Mattel is getting into the videogame business with the launch of Mattel Game Studios, which it says "will develop, publish, and operate original interactive experiences inspired by Mattel’s portfolio of iconic brands." But the approach it's taking to that task is rather different from what we've seen in the past.

The launch of the new division actually arises from a previous enterprise, Mattel163, a joint venture with NetEase that Mattel took full control of earlier this year. Founded in 2019, Mattel163 published a handful of digital card games for mobile devices including Phase 10: World Tour, Skip-Bo, and of course, Uno.

Mattel's acquisition of the company "advances Mattel’s vision to extend physical play to the virtual world by creating digital games and experiences that drive sustained engagement for fans of all ages," a line from the press blast (via Game Developer ) I include just because I think we should all have the opportunity to enjoy it.

Anyway, you can expect games of that sort to continue. Another Uno-based game, Uno Wild, is now in soft launch for mobile devices, and Mattel Game Studios is also working on a new game based on Hot Wheels. But Mattel Game Studios is moving beyond mobile development, and this is the part I find interesting: The company says it also plans to release "original experiences on creator platforms such as Roblox and Fortnite."

That's a reflection of the state of mainstream gaming, and where at least some of it is headed.

We've seen heavyweights like Amazon and Hasbro try to elbow their way onto the mainstream gaming scene to mixed results; at the same time, Roblox players spent more than 10 billion hours in Roblox every month in 2025—more than player hours spent on Steam, PlayStation, and Fortnite combined —while Fortnite, underpinned by the Unreal Engine, is attracting crossover deals with some of the most massive media companies on the planet, and actively pursuing an entirely new development ecosystem built on its technology.

So maybe you're not interested in a Poochie Pals extraction shooter (or whatever ) but the odds are good you're also probably not interested in Brainrot. Lots of other people (mostly kids) are, though, and guess where they're getting it? In a way, Mattel's approach echoes that of Amazon and Hasbro, but without the millions of dollars sunk into chasing conventional markets.

And Brainrot may be where it starts, but not necessarily where it ends. Writing about the Ready or Not-inspired shooter TTK on Roblox, PC Gamer's Morgan Park said it's a reminder "that Roblox games don't have to be terrible. " Not that TTK is an especially outstanding experience, but as Morgan wrote, "it's fine, it's free, but it's also about as good as a number of Steam shooters that release regularly.

" I have no doubt that for a lot of companies whose primary concern is leveraging new markets, that'll be plenty good enough.

If it works—and I have no reason to doubt—then I wouldn't be surprised to see other companies opting to pursue gamers not on Steam or game consoles, but on platforms like Roblox. And not just companies who aren't traditionally into videogames: Less than a year after announcing an all-in effort to salvage Payday 3, after all, Starbreeze seems to be focused primarily on bringing the property to—you guessed it— Roblox and Fortnite.

Apple’s updates to the OS 26 operating systems this year have been a nonstop flood of security fixes. You can either blame AI for finding them or thank AI for helping fix them, but either way, the sheer number of security updates released this year has been a huge escalation over prior years.

Today, Apple released iOS and iPadOS 26.6.1 along with macOS 26.6.2. The number discrepancy is because macOS got a 26.6.1 release to fix a security vulnerability that only affects macOS. These updates only fix security flaws, and Apple’s Security Release page lists about 20, including on particularly impactful WebKit update that addresses eight CVE entries on its own.

For those with older iPhones or iPads that cannot run the iOS/iPadOS 26, Apple has released iOS and iPadOS 18.7.10 which fixes most of the same security flaws and many, many more: There are almost 100 security fixes in the 18.7.10 update.

If you’re in the beta test group, you can update to this latest version by opening Settings > General > Software Update.

articles.title: Tim Cook did his best, for better or worse
articles.subtitle: Macworld The days are counting down, and a 15-year era is drawing to a close. On September 1, Tim Cook will step back from his current role as Apple CEO, settling for a somewhat quieter job as executive chairman, and it will be time to evaluate his place in...
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
The days are counting down, and a 15-year era is drawing to a close. On September 1, Tim Cook will step back from his current role as Apple CEO, settling for a somewhat quieter job as executive chairman, and it will be time to evaluate his place in corporate history. There’s every reason to think historians will be relatively kind.

I say relatively, because the bar for decency in Cook’s field is low. If we look at his peers and rivals, we find a mixed bag, to put it politely: few sane commentators would have Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg or Sam Altman on their list of 10 Nicest Dudes Who Should Definitely Have Access To Political Power.

Much as tech in the 60s and 70s attracted hippies and idealists, tech in the 2010s and 2020s seems to have become the province of, well, the sort of people who think it’s a gotcha to point out that humans consume food.

To a degree, such a mindset—the disposition, we might say, to build and stock an underground shelter rather than work to prevent the catastrophe it’s designed for—is an inevitable result of being extremely rich and running an extremely large business in an extremely competitive market.

Tim Cook is a billionaire, and it would be absurd to expect billionaires to be soft-hearted or prone to wild attacks of no-strings generosity. You don’t become a billionaire unless you’re at least above average in the ruthlessness department.

But is Cook a good and decent man? If that sounds like an odd question to ask, please note that I’m not the one asking. In a micro-interview last week, Cook fielded two questions from CBS News’ Jo Ling Kent, and while he technically didn’t answer either of them, he did put forward an interesting metric by which his legacy could be evaluated.

Kent: As you look back on your time as CEO, in a word, what have you stood for?

Cook: In my view, your legacy is described by others, not by yourself. I hope that people say I was a good and decent man. And if they say that at the end of the day, I [will] feel like I have achieved something.

That’s not one word, Tim. But I get where you’re coming from.

Will we say he was a good and decent man? I’m not sure. Cook’s inner decency is almost as elusive as his interview responses. He has the vibe of decency. He comes across as a nice guy, the sort of boss who remembers people’s names and contributes handsomely to going-away gifts. But that’s enormously subjective.

Those who’ve actually worked with him (I will note here for clarity that he and I have never even been in the same room) will be able to judge better than the rest of us. But what can we learn from his actions?

The truth is that Cook’s actions have not always been those of an unfailingly good and decent man. On his watch, for example, Apple’s treatment of retail and support employees has come in for severe criticism. At one meeting, Cook himself declined to answer questions submitted by the AppleToo activist group, whose leaders understandably said they did not feel heard.

The company has reportedly blocked pay surveys, likely breaking the law; it has discouraged unionization and, coincidentally or not, closed the first U.S. Apple Store to achieve this. Conditions in Apple’s Asian supply chain, of course, are a serious issue.

On the other hand, all the things above were true when Cook took the top job, and while he hasn’t solved them, he has tried. Apple published a list of suppliers for the first time in 2012, months after he became CEO; in 2020, he put a major supplier on probation for breaking the company’s code of conduct. Apple’s environmental record, while still far from perfect, vastly improved under the tenure of Lisa P.

Jackson, whom Cook hired in 2013 until she retired earlier this year. We even got to enjoy/endure the CEO bantering with Mother Nature at the iPhone 15 launch event.

To be clear, many of the reforms we’ve seen in the Cook era have been forced on him by regulators or bad PR, but there remains a sense that while Steve Jobs, for one, would have refused to give in, Cook is more conciliatory. It also appears that Cook has far more of an urge to do the right thing than his famous predecessor.

In 2014, the Mac Observer reported that he responded angrily to a shareholder question about whether focusing on sustainability was good for the company’s bottom line. “When we work on making our devices accessible by the blind, I don’t consider the bloody ROI,” he said. “If you want me to do things only for ROI reasons, you should get out of this stock.

” It takes a lot of courage for a CEO to go after the shareholders.

articles.title: Hands-On with Computer History: OpenAI’s Take on Agent Memory
articles.subtitle: Late yesterday, OpenAI revealed the sort of automation catnip I love: Computer History. It’s a new feature for Pro, Business, and Enterprise subscribers that creates continuity for ChatGPT and Codex by converting the actions you take on your Mac into...
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Late yesterday, OpenAI revealed the sort of automation catnip I love: Computer History. It’s a new feature for Pro, Business, and Enterprise subscribers that creates continuity for ChatGPT and Codex by converting the actions you take on your Mac into Markdown memory files that serve as context for subsequent interactions.

The idea is that with the additional context, ChatGPT and Codex will better understand your requests, requiring you to provide less detail up front while getting better results. Anyone familiar with OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and similar projects will know where this is going.

Here’s how it works.

Computer History is currently a Mac-only feature that is turned off by default, so if you want to try it, head to the Integrations section of the desktop app’s settings and toggle it on. History entries can be cleared individually, too. Before you get started, ChatGPT explains that you can pause or clear your history and manage the apps and websites that Computer History accesses at any time.

I excluded Passwords, 1Password, and Keychain Access to start and may add to that list as I use the feature more and get a better sense for the sort of information that it collects.

That opening alert also says you agree to pause Computer History during video and audio calls with others to avoid recording them without their consent. I appreciate the reminder that recording people without consent is something you shouldn’t do and is even illegal in some places, but as with the many meeting summarization tools on the market, I doubt that very many people will heed the warning and comply even though doing so is just a click of the menu bar away.

Still, I appreciate the alert up front, because turning Computer History on requires trust that the information won’t be misused by OpenAI. I’m sure that’s a bridge too far for some, but one of the most frustrating parts of using a tool like Codex is explaining yourself over and over. Every thread is like Groundhog Day for an agent, and while there are techniques that help provide continuity, making it automatic with Computer History is an exciting prospect.

If you’re intrigued by the potential, it pays to read OpenAI’s documentation and understand how the feature works. First of all, Computer History is not the same as Chronicle, a retired research preview feature that relied on taking screenshots as you worked.

In contrast, Computer History records interaction events but not screenshots, audio, or private web browsing sessions, according to OpenAI’s documentation. In practice, what that means is that as you work, ChatGPT will record your switches from app to app and what you’re doing in apps. Here’s what it’s captured as I started work on this story:

As you can see, every 10 minutes, ChatGPT creates a brief, timestamped summary of what I’ve been doing and lists the apps I’ve used by their icons. If I hover over an entry, I can immediately delete it or open the source file in the Finder for more detail on the information that ChatGPT is collecting.

Each entry in Computer History is a Markdown file with YAML front matter that includes a title, description, and list of the apps you’ve used followed by a structured memory document. Here, you’ll see a summary of what you’ve done:

The user continued writing computer history. md in Obsidian’s MacStories Vault, refining the section that explains how Computer History differs from the earlier Chronicle preview and adding a practical description of what the feature records while the user works.

The user referenced the OpenAI Learn Computer History documentation in Safari, briefly exchanged messages with Federico Viticci, checked ChatGPT/Codex settings, and then opened MacStories Images to queue a screenshot named CleanShot 2026-08-14 at 06. 08. 44@2x. png for upload. The upload was queued by the end of the segment, but no completed upload or copied Markdown image link was observed.

You’ll also find details that ChatGPT deems important and non-obvious, such as the following:

Important non-obvious context about the user MacStories Vault - Obsidian vault where the Computer History article draft was active. computer history. md - active note being drafted for the Computer History article. CleanShot 2026-08-14 at 06. 08. 44@2x. png - screenshot selected from @ Screenshots and queued in MacStories Images near the end of the window.

MacStories Images - internal Safari image uploader used for the screenshot; the page showed one queued item and an Upload 1 control. Federico Viticci - Messages conversation briefly active during the writing session. ChatGPT/Codex settings - ChatGPT app showed settings around 10:08Z, likely related to the same Computer History article context.

Important non-obvious context about the user

MacStories Vault - Obsidian vault where the Computer History article draft was active.

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Another endorsement of Apple’s approach

articles.title: Pokopia Fan Figures Out How To Get Limited-TIme Pokémon Without Messing With Switch 2 Settings
articles.subtitle: Pokémon Pokopia Pokémon Pokopia has limited-time events that allow you to recruit special ‘mons to your towns. These only happen during set dates and times, so if you want to get those Pokémon, you have to either play the life sim during specific dates,...
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Pokémon Pokopia

Pokémon Pokopia has limited-time events that allow you to recruit special ‘mons to your towns. These only happen during set dates and times, so if you want to get those Pokémon, you have to either play the life sim during specific dates, or go into your Switch 2’s settings and “time travel” by changing your system’s internal clock. However, a player has found a complex workaround that will allow you to recruit special Pokémon without having to wait or mess around with your system’s circadian rhythm.

Redditor ArcadiaCitizen_ has figured out a way that you can exploit some already existing systems in Pokopia to spawn Pokémon who you usually can’t find unless you’re playing during an event.

To pull this off, you’ll need to have the Mysterious Goggles, which allow you to access cloud islands, or areas made by other players. Once there, you can take photos and use Pokopia’s 3D printer in Pokémon Centers to essentially create most items in the game, provided you have enough Pokémetal or Rare Pokémetal for each item. Game Freak and Koei Tecmo have created a cloud island that has practically every item you can imagine in Pokopia, including items that are specific to the habitats of event Pokémon.

3D printing them will allow you to recruit monsters like the Jumpluff family, Sableye, and Jirachi, rather than having to wait until their respective events. However, you will need a Nintendo Switch Online membership to access online features. The island code ArcadiaCitizen_ was able to use is 6DXL PD6F.

When Pokopia first launched earlier this year, it received some criticism for having time-limited Pokémon recruitment windows, given that a lot of fans still hadn’t managed to get a Switch 2 by the time the game launched in March and didn’t know if they would be able to before those windows closed. Now, it seems like there are multiple ways to get around this restriction, whether the developers intended them or not.

articles.title: 2024’s Greatest Roguelike Is a Must-Play on Xbox Game Pass
articles.subtitle: The indie smash elevates that cheatin' feeling into high art Related In the original Star Wars, Han Solo says of the Millennium Falcon, “She might not look like much, kid.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
The indie smash elevates that cheatin' feeling into high art

Related

In the original Star Wars, Han Solo says of the Millennium Falcon, “She might not look like much, kid. But she’s got it where it counts.” The same is also true of Balatro, the roguelike from solo developer LocalThunk that took the gaming world by storm back in 2024. It was nominated for five Game Awards and took home three, and had sold a whopping 5 million copies as of January 2025.

Balatro may look like a simple riff on poker, but beneath its pixel-art surface lies an engine for boundless experimentation. Your task is to play several poker hands of five or fewer cards to beat a score requirement that gets higher each round. There are eight antes, or levels, and each one contains three rounds. Depending on the luck of the draw, you can play any traditional poker hand you like, ranging from a simple high card to a straight flush.

It’s an old aphorism that “you can’t change the hand you’re dealt. ” In Balatro, not only can you change the hand you’re dealt, your success absolutely depends on it. When you visit the in-game shop between rounds, you can buy more cards for your hand, making it lopsided with face cards. (Or threes, I guess, if you’re some kind of sicko. ) And the customization doesn’t stop there.

There are also tarot cards, which add extra points or increased point multipliers to the cards in your deck. Planet cards, meanwhile, increase the points you get for specific poker hands. Over time, that could mean that an easy-to-get hand like a pair actually earns you far more points than a technically better hand, like four-of-a-kind.

As you progress through each ante, you’ll want to pick a lane and just run one or two hand types to maximize your score.

But it’s the jokers that allow Balatro to evolve from “poker with a gimmick” into an enchanting number-go-up machine that will captivate you for hours on end. You start each run with five joker slots, but depending on the circumstances, you can end up with plenty more than that. There are 150 different jokers in the game, and each one has a wildly different effect.

Some are short-lived, like the Popcorn joker, which adds +20 to your multiplier, though the value diminishes by four points each round. Others are absurdly strong but hard to come by, like Cavendish, which adds a 3x multiplier to your entire hand.

In the early rounds, you’re free to experiment. But if you want to get past ante 8 — or beyond that into the infinite play mode that requires truly bonkers scores — you’ll need to find jokers that multiply your multiplier (like Cavendish, Gros Michel, and Baron) to send your points into the stratosphere. There are even jokers that duplicate the effects of other jokers (like Blueprint and Brainstorm).

The way you organize your jokers at the top of the screen is important, too. Balatro demands that you respect the order of operations: put your points jokers to the far left, then additional mult, and then Xmult.

I’ll admit that sounds very complicated on paper, and at first, it kind of is. Early rounds of Balatro are all about learning through failure, but discovering wacky new jokers and experimenting while you vibe to the groovy tunes keeps it fun the whole time.

Balatro becomes a transcendent experience once you’ve acquainted yourself with its systems enough to make you feel like you're breaking the game, even when you're playing it precisely as it was designed to be played. Despite the snarky jester Jimbo heckling you every time you lose, eventually, Balatro will make you feel like a once-in-a-generation math genius.

While Balatro is wonderful on a handheld device like a Nintendo Switch or even your phone, I would warn you against dancing with the devil in this way. This is not a game you want to bring anywhere near your bed. It will wreak absolute havoc on your sleep hygiene, even if you have a great time doing it. Taking Balatro for a spin on Xbox Game Pass is the best way to see if it clicks for you. Just don’t say I didn’t warn you.

In addition to Game Pass, Balatro is available now on Android, iOS, Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X.

articles.title: Big Walk: A Good Hang with Friends
articles.subtitle: I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it. And because most of my gaming is done solo, I initially tuned out most of the game’s post-launch headlines. Still, Big Walk is published by Panic, which has a great track record for finding and publishing great indie games, so I decided to give it a try earlier this week. And you know what? I love it.

Big Walk is about as low-key as a puzzle game gets in the best possible way. Co-op is the only mode, so you’ll need to coordinate a time to play it with a friend or group. One person takes the lead, setting up the session and inviting the others. The process is far simpler than trying to find a time that works for everyone in your group.

As players join, you’re dropped into a space to wait for the others and explore a little. This lobby space is where you’ll learn the game’s controls, too. Big Walk supports keyboard and mouse input as well as a controller, which is what I used, playing on an M4 Max MacBook Pro.

Once you get your bearings, it’s time to exit the lobby and start exploring. That exploration is core to what Big Walk is all about. You aren’t told what to do, but there are just enough clues to push you forward, figuring out the goals on your own without too much trouble.

I played using AirPods Pro 3, and the game made great use of their mics and speakers, simulating the environments we were in. Closed spaces were echoey, and speech was distant and faint when we were separated. Sound even becomes part of the mechanic in some puzzles, such as an early one where you have to look through an open window to hear each other properly and help guide the other player’s actions.

That cooperation is the key part of the game’s loop. You may see how to solve Big Walk’s puzzles on your own, but implementing the solution will require you and a companion to work together.

The togetherness of it all extends beyond the puzzles, too. Big Walk’s environment (at least in the early stages) is mountainous with large rocks and trees that make it possible to get separated from others. Add to that day and night cycles where it’s almost impossible to see where you’re going at night without a light, and you have every incentive not to wander off on your own without a plan for how to reconnect.

I’ve played through Big Walk’s first couple of sections, and it was a blast. The puzzles were clever and challenging without being frustrating, but most of all, I enjoyed working through them with someone else. There’s no time pressure or monsters lurking around corners – just puzzles and a chance to chat.

Ultimately, that’s what makes Big Walk work. It’s a good hang built against the backdrop of a beautiful landscape and low-key, fun challenges. I highly recommend giving it a try.

Big Walk, which supports crossplay and 2–12 players, is available on the Mac App Store for $14.99. The game is also on Steam, the Switch 2, and PS5.

Hello there

Related

Star Wars Zero Company is the next big-ticket video game set in a galaxy far, far away. It's out next week, and on Monday publisher EA shared a new, final trailer for the turn-based tactics game ahead of its release. The trailer includes shots from cutscenes and of its XCOM-like gameplay, but fans were more excited that the trailer confirmed the return of one of their favorite characters.

At around the 1:45-minute mark of the below trailer, Captain Rex, clad in his iconic helmet and armor, makes a cameo appearance. He's only on screen for a brief second, but that was enough to get Star Wars fans hyped. "REX! MY BROTHER! MY BOY! MY LAD!" reads one of the top comments on YouTube.

Captain Rex debuted in the 2008 The Clone Wars film ahead of its animated series follow-up, serving primarily alongside Jedi Anakin Skywalker and Ahsoka Tano. He's been a staple of Star Wars media about that seminal conflict, and has been a featured player in later series like Star Wars Rebels and Star Wars: The Bad Batch.

Rex, like all clone troopers in the animated shows, has been voiced by Dee Bradley Baker. We knew Baker would be in Zero Company after the stacked cast was fully revealed last month, but he was only confirmed to be voicing a different clone trooper, Trick. As such, it's not clear how much of a role Rex will have in the game, or if Baker will be voicing any other surprise clones.

Anakin will also be popping up in Star Wars Zero Company, but how much of a role he'll have to play is also unknown. Zero Company primarily follows a group of misfits covertly working with the Galactic Republic.

Star Wars Zero Company has been described as "Star Wars XCOM" and, after 10 hours with it, that moniker rings true. "It's shaping up to be the best version of XCOM-style squad-based tactics yet," Polygon's Josh Broadwell wrote in his preview. You won't have to wait too long to check it out for yourself: Star Wars Zero Company will be released Aug. 27 for $49.99 on Windows PC and $59.99 on PS5 and Xbox Series X.

SpaceXAI and Cursor are in the process of becoming a single company, but first, the two firms are releasing an all-new iPhone and Mac app called Grok Bot.

According to SpaceXAI’s announcement, Grok Bot is a new kind of AI agent described as “AI teammates you can give real work to.”

Each Bot gets its own computer, then signs into the apps and services you already use to take on work across inboxes and other tools.

articles.title: Siri will sometimes summarize webpages and videos from within Safari and YouTube apps
articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.title: The Utility App Flood Won’t Last
articles.subtitle: The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.

Since then, veteran developers are releasing new apps and updating existing ones faster than ever, and new developers are releasing their first apps in droves. Today, supply is dramatically up, demand is flat, and quality is seemingly simultaneously up and down, depending on where you look.

How these forces play out long-term is anyone’s guess, but it’s worth examining because, just as Federico’s link to Bryan Irace’s post about agentic coding tools foreshadowed the rise of tools like Codex and Claude Code, today’s trends are sparks that have the potential to become tomorrow’s App Store wildfires or simply fizzle out.

Utility apps are on the front lines of this change. The TechCrunch story I linked in April picked up on this trend:

Another interesting tidbit from Appfigures is that the Utilities app category moved up the top five chart.

If anything, the trend has accelerated in the months since.

It’s not surprising at all that utility apps have taken off. They’ve been a staple of new developers since long before agents came along. That’s because many are UI wrappers around command line tools. That isn’t a knock against the developers of those apps; most users don’t want to open Terminal to convert a video or audio file to another format using ffmpeg, for example. By building a great UI around command line tools, developers have made them far easier to use.

However, the relative simplicity and narrow scope of many utility apps have made them a natural fit for AI agents, too. That’s why the App Store (and my inbox) is deluged with Mac menu bar and single-screen iPhone and iPad utility apps.

On the one hand, the abundance of utilities has been great for users. More choice means you’re more likely to find the app that perfectly fits your needs.

On the other hand, though, I don’t think what’s happening in the category is sustainable and expect to see it dramatically shift again in the coming months. As we’ve seen from reporting by The New York Times, app supply is outstripping demand by orders of magnitude, which will drive down prices. That alone is likely to cause the utility app market to shrink. But there’s more to it than that.

Remember, the demand shifts that The New York Times reported, based on Sensor Tower numbers, are for the entire App Store, where download numbers have grown 2-3% this year and last. I expect utility downloads to actually shrink in the coming months – again, because of agents.

Utilities, especially simple ones, are exactly the sorts of apps that are becoming trivially easy for power users – the very users these utilities are made for – to create themselves. From frontier labs‘ model improvements to a growing number of app-building tools from those same labs and third parties, it’s never been easier to build a web or native app yourself.

And although I agree with people, like Nilay Patel, who say the notion that everyone will build their own software is overblown, the utility market is different. Your average person is not downloading apps to adjust the frame rate and file format of a video or downloading YouTube videos to watch later.

But those are exactly the sort of things that people who are using agents are doing with them, whether they’re having an agent do those things directly via a command line tool in an app like Codex or Claude Code or building an app to do the same thing. That’s going to put even more pressure on the category.

That said, I think there will always be a cohort of users who would rather pay for an app than build it themselves, so I’m not predicting the demise of utilities in general – just the end of today’s frothy market. I also think there remains a place for simple utilities that solve hard problems with clever solutions. Not every utility is a UI wrapper for a terminal command. Plenty of apps feature original solutions or thoughtful and unconventional remixes of disparate tools.

Utilities aren’t going away, but just like other App Store deluges, the trend will recede. It’s just that this time, it’s likely to flip faster than usual.

The Analogue Pocket is already one of the slickest ways to revisit Nintendo 's Game Boy era without digging a scratched-up handheld out of a closet.

The premium handheld plays original Game Boy, Game Boy Color, and Game Boy Advance cartridges using FPGA hardware, all on a razor-sharp 3.5-inch screen. Basically, it’s a very fancy Game Boy built to make old games look great.

Now, lifestyle brand Supreme has gotten its hands on it, and naturally, it looks cool as hell.

Supreme's Analogue Pocket comes in red and 24K gold

Supreme revealed two new Analogue Pocket variants as part of its fall/winter 2026 collection: one finished in the brand’s signature glossy red and another plated in 24K gold.

Both versions use a unibody aluminum shell and feature Supreme branding on the front and rear. Underneath all that fashion-world excess, though, they appear to be the same Analogue Pocket hardware you can already buy.

Supreme hasn’t announced pricing for either model yet. For comparison, the standard Analogue Pocket currently sells for $239.99. Given Analogue and Supreme’s mutual enthusiasm for limited releases, it’s probably safe to expect these to be both more expensive and harder to get.

The Pockets aren’t Supreme’s only gadget collaborations this season, either. Its fall/winter lineup also includes a Supreme-branded Kodak Super 8 camera, Dyson V12 Detect vacuum, JBL Go 5 speaker, Jamo Capsule light, and wireless microphone setup, among the usual assortment of clothes and accessories.

Supreme says the collection launches Aug. 20.

Should you buy an Analogue Pocket?

If you’ve got old Game Boy cartridges lying around, the Pocket is one of the coolest ways to play them.

Instead of conventional software emulation, the Pocket uses FPGA hardware to closely recreate vintage systems and run original Game Boy, Game Boy Color, and Game Boy Advance carts. Its biggest selling point is the gorgeous 3.5-inch, 1600-by-1440 display, which Polygon praised for its sharp scaling and excellent retro-style screen filters when the system first launched. The review was less enthusiastic about the vertical design, which can be uncomfortable in larger hands.

OpenFPGA support also lets the Pocket run community-made cores for other classic systems, making it more versatile than it was at launch.

The Supreme editions won’t change how it plays, though. Unless you really want the red shell or 24K gold flex, the standard $239.99 Pocket gets you the same core experience — though Supreme enthusiasts appear to be getting a custom boot screen with the New York brand's familiar box logo.

articles.title: Review: SuperDuper! 4 gets a stem-to-stern revamp, but is just as seaworthy as ever
articles.subtitle: Backups, as any computer user knows, are worth their weight in gold. If it isn’t backed up, it might as well might not exist. That’s why I have for years trusted ShirtPocket’s SuperDuper!…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Backups, as any computer user knows, are worth their weight in gold. If it isn’t backed up, it might as well might not exist. That’s why I have for years trusted ShirtPocket’s SuperDuper! to ensure that all my data is safe and sound. And now, for the first time in a very long time, the venerable backup utility has gotten a top-to-bottom update that brings it into the modern era without sacrificing any of the features—and, most importantly, the reliability—that its users have come to depend on.

While SuperDuper! 4 may look like an entirely new beast, its history has stuck around. It still explains what it’s doing in plain English. It still allows you to make complete, bootable backups. It still has its excellent Smart Update option to optimize the copying process.

But it’s gotten some significant updates too. There’s a new interface, for starters, which conforms to Apple’s current Liquid Glass aesthetic, love it or hate it. It’s a bit of a shock to the system after so long without a change, but it’s hard to deny that the old look had grown somewhat antiquated. The result is an app that makes backups as simple and straightforward as they should be, so that anyone can figure it out: click here to set your destination, choose what method, and click Go.

The changes to SuperDuper! 4 also run more than just skin deep. For example, it’s considerably faster than the previous version—up to an order magnitude faster using the new Turbo implementation of Smart Update, according to Shirt Pocket. That’s borne out in my real-world usage. For example, my last nightly backup of 20.55GB took less than 4 minutes.

There are new capabilities here, too. A new Preview feature lets you perform a dry run of your copy job, letting you see every file that will be changed without actually doing any of it. With a new background helper app, copies won’t interrupt whatever you’re doing. And there’s Shortcuts support, so you can run a workflow when your copy job is completed—or even have one of your shortcuts kick off a copy job.

I’ve been using betas of SuperDuper! 4 for a month or so now, and what’s impressed me most is how much it maintains that set-it-and-forget-it strength of the previous versions. The most important thing for a backup is that element of reliability, so when I open up the app and see “31 successful in a row” note, I know that my data is right where it should be.

And if something goes wrong, it’s easier than ever to see what happened: click on a failed job and you’ll get the details, including an Apple Intelligence-powered summary of the job. (You can get that for completed jobs too. )

There are way more features here too, ones that I just don’t have much reason to use for my purposes, but might just well be what you’re looking for. For example, copy rules that let you handle certain files and folders in granular ways, such as excluding certain ones from backups; support for any file system that macOS understands; and there’s support for multiple copy jobs at the same time, even for those that are scheduled.

Backup apps may not be the most exciting software category, but I dare you to find one that’s more crucial. For me, SuperDuper! has done the job for years and I’ve never had any reason to complain about it. Nothing about that seems poised to change with version 4.

SuperDuper! 4 requires macOS 14 (Sonoma) or later. A free trial version lets you make unlimited full erase backups, but to unlock the rest of the features requires a one-time payment of $43.95. There’s also an upgrade discount for owners of SuperDuper 3 of up to 30 percent. (And, if you bought version 3 very recently, you may be able to get version 4 for free.) And good news: if you need to run backups on older systems, SuperDuper 3 is sticking around.

For everybody who’s already backing up their Macs, SuperDuper! 4 may offer some new features and speed increases that will make the process even smoother. For those of you who aren’t yet…what are you waiting for?

articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality.

AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation. Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems.

articles.content:
At this weekend's huge fighting game tournament, Melee ended with a strange scene

Related

Decades after its release, Super Smash Bros. Melee for the GameCube still has a very active competitive scene, with regular major tournaments and even a custom-built emulator that enables smooth online play. Thanks to the long-running nature of Melee ’s competitive scene, we’ve been gifted plenty of colorful characters over the years.

Two of these top-level mainstays, Juan “Hungrybox” DeBiedma and Cody Schwab, were at the center of a strange snafu that happened in the grand finals of this weekend’s massive Florida-based tournament, CEO.

The strange happening came as Hungrybox and Schwab faced off in their fifteenth match of the tournament. Hungrybox had previously beaten Schwab in the winners' finals match, sending Schwab to the losers’ bracket (most fighting game tournaments are double elimination, meaning you need to lose two sets to be out of the event). As the two players battled it out in the final game of the tournament, Hungrybox was up three stocks to two when the following happened.

For those who don’t understand what’s going on, Schwab appears to recoil from something, which causes him to stop playing. The commentators are unsure about what’s happening and assume Schwab’s controller is malfunctioning. Hungrybox looks concerned, as his eyes dart between his opponent and the screen.

However, Hungrybox’s confusion doesn’t keep him from sneaking in two hits on his opponent mid-conversation, causing Schwab to clearly yell, “What are you doing? ” Out of context, the sequence looks hilarious and quickly went viral on social media.

As for what actually happened here, Schwab wrote on X, “For the people asking about game 15, Hbox got a little too hype and it shook the hell out of my chair, but I also don’t think I would’ve won anyways. I just asked for a reset given that I got completely thrown off. Genuinely no harm no foul.” Right before Schwab stops playing, you can see Hungrybox scooting his seat back, which appears to be what threw Schwab off.

Recommended For You

That said, the situation is extremely unusual because pausing a match for any reason is quite frowned upon in competitive play. In Super Smash Bros. (or any other fighting game), if a player stops for any reason, they are generally expected to forfeit the round or match, even for something out of their control like controller issues. Because of this, Schwab stopping play and asking for a position reset has garnered quite a bit of criticism.

Both players have had colorful moments over the past week. Just a week ago, Hungrybox popped off so aggressively after a tournament win that he literally fainted. Meanwhile, Schwab apparently had food poisoning while competing at CEO, but still managed to reach the grand finals. 25 years later, Super Smash Bros. Melee shows little sign of slowing down, with viral moments fueling at least a bit of that momentum.

Even after two decades, Melee glitches reign supreme.

articles.subtitle: Wispr Flow users on Mac can now access Notetaker, an AI-powered meeting assistant that uses calendars, connected apps, and personal dictionaries to provide additional context for transcripts, summaries, and notes. Here are the details.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Wispr Flow users on Mac can now access Notetaker, an AI-powered meeting assistant that uses calendars, connected apps, and personal dictionaries to provide additional context for transcripts, summaries, and notes. Here are the details.

Wispr Notetaker now available for Mac

If you’re unfamiliar with Wispr Flow, it is one of the leading voice-to-text AI tools for a growing number of users who feel comfortable using voice to compose messages, emails, documents, and other text instead of typing.

Granted, voice-based interactions are not practical in every environment. Still, Wispr Flow ’s rapidly growing user base (which the company said in March was expanding by 40% month over month) suggests that AI-powered dictation tools may become mainstream faster than many expected, or give them credit for.

Until now, Wispr has offered a single product, which polishes up messy speech and turns it into “clear, polished writing in every app.”

Today, the company is expanding its lineup with Notetaker, a smart, AI-powered meeting assistant, transcriber, and summarizer. The new tool is built directly into Wispr Flow and appears as a new item in the app’s left-hand sidebar.

As Wispr CEO and co-founder Tanay Kothari notes (no pun intended):

“Nobody reads meeting transcripts. But everyone acts on them. The transcript feeds the summary, the summary feeds the follow-up email, the recap goes to whoever missed the call. You’ve learned to give the notes a quick once-over before trusting them, because sometimes a name is wrong or an action item is assigned to the wrong person.”

In other words, while the transcript itself may have limited value to some, accurately extracting the key details, decisions, and action items from it can be more useful to a broader set of users.

Notetaker also briefs users before meetings by gathering relevant information from their notes and the web, with each line linked to its source. More broadly, it draws context from calendars and connected apps such as Slack.

During meetings, Notetaker provides a live transcript so the user can quickly check back on what was said. Once the meeting ends, it processes the full recording again with additional context, which Wispr says improves the final transcript and the summaries, decisions, key dates, and action items generated from it.

Afterward, users can ask questions about their full meeting history, with answers linked to the moment when the relevant information was discussed. Notetaker can also catch users up on portions of a meeting they missed or were not paying attention to.

In addition to sharing Wispr Flow ’s custom dictionary, which helps with accuracy for acronyms, names, product names, and beyond, Wispr Notetaker “draws on the apps you connect, like Slack, and your calendar, to understand what this particular conversation is about,” says Kothari.

This also helps with automatic speaker attribution, which is particularly useful for meetings with several participants.

Wispr Notetaker transcribes meetings based on on-device audio capture, rather than joining calls as a separate participant.

It works across multiple meeting platforms, including Zoom, Google Meet, Teams, and Slack huddles, and has MCP support, allowing users to pull transcripts, summaries, and notes into Claude, ChatGPT, and custom agents or workflows.

Wispr Notetaker is available beginning today on Mac, with a Windows version in development.

articles.title: Post Malone Used His $2 Million Lord Of The Rings Card In An Actual Game Of Magic
articles.subtitle: Magic: The Gathering Post Malone Do you know why I respect Post Malone over any other “famous” card collector? Because mans actually plays with his cards.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Magic: The Gathering Post Malone

Do you know why I respect Post Malone over any other “famous” card collector? Because mans actually plays with his cards. During an episode of Game Knights, a Magic: The Gathering Actual Play YouTube series, Postie whipped out his The One Ring card—the only card of its kind printed by MTG developer Wizards of the Coast which he paid over $2 million for, took it partially out of its protective slab on a game table that had earlier been subjected to drink spillage—and played it.

Post Malone just used his "The One Ring" card in an actual game of Magic: The Gathering 👀 He famously purchased the 1-of-1 card from a Toronto collector for $2 million in 2023. pic.twitter.com/z606gZSZxN — Fanatics Collect (@Collect) August 15, 2026

Post Malone just used his "The One Ring" card in an actual game of Magic: The Gathering 👀

He famously purchased the 1-of-1 card from a Toronto collector for $2 million in 2023. pic.twitter.com/z606gZSZxN

— Fanatics Collect (@Collect) August 15, 2026

Post Malone is a well-documented MTG fan with his own Secret Lair collaboration and charity tournaments. But actually playing the literal holy grail of Magic cards is another thing entirely, speaking to a deep and true love of the game that goes beyond having an expensive thing just to have it. Something I don’t think fake Pokémon fan Logan Paul can lay claim to.

Despite Posty letting the One Ring see actual play time (you can check out his deck here ), the true hero at the table was Rachel Weeks and her Notary Hobbits deck. Her deck makes use of Notary Hobbits’ ability to copy itself and turn other hobbit cards into mana.

With it and help from a card that essentially exponentially increased her mana pool, she was able to play a card that let her indiscriminately kill her opponents’ creatures and snatch creature cards out of their graveyards for the low price of free.

When your opponents’ graveyard becomes your deck, and you have the ability to generate massive amounts of mana to pay for big-ass, powerful-ass creatures, all kinds of shenanigans became possible. These synergies made her the biggest threat at the table for a good portion of the game, which absolutely delighted my green-mana-big-creatures-loving-ass.

Oh shit. I know what’s happening here. I’m being influenced. I’m not a Commander player; I think the games go on for too long (I’m old), the format is too big and intimidating for me, and I tend to enjoy the snappier play and forced creativity that comes from the stricter boundaries of limited formats like draft and sealed.

But watching this show and seeing the crazy shit you can get up to when you build a deck out of the nigh-unlimited card pool that Commander permits is powerfully seductive. Kinda like the One Ring itself.

It was a delight watching Post Malone play this game of Commander, flailing about in the earliest turns while his opponents teased him for his single creature that he wasn’t able to use effectively. But once he pulled out the One Ring, which grants him protection from all damage, things changed. Drastically.

All that earlier flailing melted away to reveal a cogent strategy with a couple of lucky topdecks for added drama. (Always pay the mana tax for Rhystic Study! ) Post Malone wound up winning the game, but I do have to rescind my respect for him because I categorically do not respect mono blue players. Sorry.

articles.title: Apple’s revolving door continues to spin, with more big-name exec changes
articles.subtitle: Macworld Apple is a large and wealthy company which employs roughly 166,000 people, so a fair amount of staff turnover is to be expected.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Apple is a large and wealthy company which employs roughly 166,000 people, so a fair amount of staff turnover is to be expected. What’s striking about the past couple of years, however, has been the number of employees leaving high-profile roles at Apple Park.

Last December, Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman discussed what he called Apple’s “biggest personnel shake-up in decades,” listing 18 big-name departures that had either happened that year or were expected to happen soon. By February, the situation had become so noticeable that CEO Tim Cook was moved to comment, sagely observing that “when people get to a certain age, some are going to retire. This is kind of a natural thing,” and insisting that the departures had been carefully orchestrated.

Whether planned or not, the high-profile personnel changes keep coming, with two more emerging this week.

First, Apple internally announced the retirement of Jennifer Bailey, who has been at the company for more than two decades, most recently as head of Pay and Wallet services. In an article revealing the move, Gurman claimed Bailey’s exit “is seen as a major loss within Apple, according to people with knowledge of the move” and that staff fears it will “presage a broader exodus of senior leaders in their 60s.

” Bailey will retire in October, although services boss Eddy Cue (current age: 61) insists she will continue in an advisory role and that a succession plan will be announced nearer the time. The current lack of a succession plan (or disinclination to reveal one) hints that this departure was less orchestrated, but there may be other factors we don’t know about.

Second, and more positively, it was announced (again by Mark Gurman at Bloomberg ) that Apple is hiring a new head of government affairs. Nate Gatten, formerly an exec at American Airlines, will take on this “delicate role,” for which his Republican ties are likely to be seen as an advantage.

A big-name signing is a win, of course, but there are complications. For one thing, this is connected to another retirement: legal chief Katherine Adams is leaving at the same time as Jennifer Bailey, and she currently serves in a similar but lower-profile role of senior VP of government affairs. For another, the need for a full-time head of government affairs reflects the murky political waters Apple currently has to navigate.

Some pundits (including this one ) have speculated that this year’s biggest personnel change–Tim Cook stepping down as CEO–will see the current boss spend more time liaising with the White House, but even Cupertino’s most famous workaholic may not be able to handle the workload on his own.

Finally, Gurman reported last week that incoming CEO John Ternus will be rehiring Laura Legros, who served as a vice president of hardware engineering until she retired in 2022. Legros will assume a vice president role, “working cross-functionally with different parts of the company,” according to the report.

Legros was one of Ternus’ “most trusted deputies,” Gurman reports. In 2018, she appeared during an Apple event in New York to introduce an updated MacBook Air and was also front and center for the iPad Air design, two important products in Apple’s recent history.

It’s the end of a very short road for ChatGPT Atlas, OpenAI’s dedicated web browser for Mac. OpenAI has shared details about what happens when ChatGPT Atlas shuts down this weekend.

ChatGPT is the new ChatGPT Atlas

As we reported in July, OpenAI is discontinuing its standalone Atlas browser in favor of browser tools built into the new ChatGPT desktop app. Atlas is scheduled to stop working on August 9 following a brief wind-down period.

OpenAI warns that Atlas may no longer open, browse, or support agentic workflows after that date. Because the discontinued browser will not continue receiving security updates, users will want to move to a supported alternative.

The transition may require some manual housekeeping for some. Atlas bookmarks will not transfer automatically. OpenAI recommends exporting bookmarks as an HTML file and saving important pages before Sunday’s deadline.

Cookies may have export options where available. ChatGPT conversation history is stored separately and will remain available.

AI browser alternatives

OpenAI is directing users toward the new ChatGPT desktop app. Its built-in browser supports multiple tabs, downloads, website logins, autofill, password management, extensions, and persistent browser state. However, it’s not exactly a browser-first experience.

The company recommends its Chrome extension when a task requires an existing Chrome profile, signed-in session, open tabs, or other extensions. ChatGPT’s desktop app also includes a “computer use” functionality that can optionally let it control Safari when granted permission.

There are plenty of other AI browser options on the Mac, including Comet, Dia, Opera Neon, and Aside. Anthropic is taking a similar two-track approach: Claude Code offers a sandboxed in-app browser, while its Chrome extension can work with existing logged-in sessions.

A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

articles.content:
Well, we've been hornswoggled again. They did it. They're doing it. Rockstar is, as we speak, putting the finishing touches on Grand Theft Auto 6, the Final Videogame, but icing you and me out entirely. No Xbox or PlayStation? Enjoy pressing your nose against the glass of your console-owning neighbours as they find themselves delighted and transformed by the world's first $500,000,000,000,000 entertainment product.

I say: no. Not today, Sam (or maybe Dan) Houser. Every day, I am going to add a new mod to Grand Theft Auto 5, until it either becomes GTA 6 or collapses under its own terrible weight. If the mountain won't come to Muhammad, Muhammad will slowly alter a separate, but nearer mountain until it's indistinguishable from the one he wanted.

Today, day one, is mostly about learning. I have plenty of experience modding, but only really in games designed for it. I get the impression Rockstar would prefer no one change its babies, and so modding GTA 5 feels iffy and ramshackle: a process of gathering.asi files and hacky tools and crowbarring your way into the game's guts. Also, all the mods' instructions consist of a.txt file that says 'put mods'. Great. Excellent. Thank you.

It's a learning experience. So, to learn, and to start slow, I figured I would begin with something simple: a new vehicle. A fresh set of wheels to cruise the hot tarmac of Los Santos. It needed to be fast, stylish, fashionable, and stand out at least a little from the usual bric-a-brac of sedans and sports cars that litter Rockstar's fake-LA.

I settled on the HQ-16 (simplified Chinese: 红旗-16; traditional Chinese: 紅旗-16; pinyin: Hóng Qí-16; lit. 'Red Banner-16'; NATO reporting name: CH-SA-16) Chinese medium-range surface-to-air missile (SAM), developed by the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology*.

I mostly did this because I wanted to familiarise myself with tools like OpenIV and make sure I could configure a mod and a few dependencies without everything blowing up in my face. I partly did it because I wanted to expose the people of Beverly Hills to the full might of the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation and the military of Pakistan. They've been coddled for too long.

Even more partly, I did it because a mod that was meant to change Franklin into Chester Bennington from Linkin Park kept making the game crash.

It worked. Before long, Los Santos was engulfed in waves of Shanghai Academic fire. Celebrity homes? Gone. Celebrity cars? Gone. Cops? Immolated. Their helicopters? Destroying those is literally what this vehicle is for. I was a one-man army in the truck of a regular several-men army, and the cops could do nothing to stop me. At least, until one of them attempted to pull me from my car—placing them right next to the driver's door when one of my many missiles found its way home to the small of his back.

I bet this never happened when the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology and China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation were testing this thing.

But my lessons are complete. I can mod GTA 5 without destroying anything. Today, a destructive truck. Tomorrow? Something more. Tune in to find out what.

*Thank you Wikipedia.

Liquid Glass opacity has been improved to increase readability, there's a slider for controlling the level of transparency, and changes to shadowing make it easier to tell when a window is active. Apps now have uniform toolbars, edge-to-edge sidebars, and less rounded corners, plus there are fewer icons in menu bars.

Siri has been transformed into ‌Siri‌ AI, a chatbot-style assistant that combines general world knowledge, your personal data, and onscreen awareness to answer questions about anything and find information for you. ‌Siri‌ lives in Spotlight, and you can ask questions with the new Search or Ask interface.

There's also a ‌Siri‌ app where you can chat with ‌Siri‌ and view past conversations, and on newer Macs, you can set a custom voice for ‌Siri‌ with personalized pace and expressivity. Visual Intelligence is now on the Mac so ‌Siri‌ can answer questions about what's on your screen, and a Write with ‌Siri‌ feature lets ‌Siri‌ generate text or give feedback on your writing.

There are AI photo editing tools in the Photos app, AI tab organization in Safari, an option to use AI to automatically update weak passwords in the Passwords app, and a revamped Image Playground app that can generate photorealistic images.

More on all of the new features in ‌macOS Golden Gate‌ can be found in our macOS Golden Gate roundup.
